def: The tangent at a point on a curve is the line touching it with the same slope as the curve there; the normal is the line perpendicular to the tangent at that point.
points: Find dy/dx at the given point; this is the slope m of the tangent.
Tangent equation: y - y1 = m(x - x1).
Normal is perpendicular to tangent, so its slope is -1/m.
Normal equation: y - y1 = (-1/m)(x - x1).
If dy/dx = 0, tangent is horizontal; normal is vertical (x = x1).
If dy/dx is undefined, tangent is vertical; normal is horizontal (y = y1).
formula: Tangent: y - y1 = (dy/dx)(x - x1)     Normal: y - y1 = -1/(dy/dx) (x - x1)

diagram.draw: Draw a smooth curve. Mark point P(x1, y1) on it. Draw a straight line just touching the curve at P, label it 'Tangent'. Draw another straight line through P at right angle to the tangent, label it 'Normal'.

example: Curve y = x^2 at (1,1): dy/dx = 2x = 2. Tangent: y - 1 = 2(x - 1) i.e. y = 2x - 1. Normal: y - 1 = -1/2(x - 1) i.e. x + 2y = 3.
tip: Always substitute the point into dy/dx first to get a numeric slope before writing the line equations.

def: Rate of change tells how fast a quantity changes with respect to another, usually time, and is found using derivatives.
points: Identify the quantity that is changing and write it as a function of time, e.g. V(t), A(t).
Differentiate both sides of the relation with respect to t using chain rule.
Substitute the given rate(s) and values at the required instant.
Solve the resulting equation for the unknown rate.
Keep units consistent (same time unit throughout).
Positive rate means increasing, negative rate means decreasing.
formula: dV/dt = (dV/dr) x (dr/dt)   (chain rule for related rates)

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Relation between quantities"] --> B["Differentiate wrt time t"]
  B --> C["Apply chain rule"]
  C --> D["Substitute known rate and value"]
  D --> E["Find required rate"]

example: Radius of a circle increases at 2 cm/s. Find rate of increase of area when r = 5 cm. A = pi r^2, dA/dt = 2 pi r (dr/dt) = 2 pi(5)(2) = 20 pi cm^2/s.
tip: Write down the given rate and the rate asked for clearly before differentiating; this avoids sign and substitution mistakes.

def: A function is increasing on an interval if its value rises as x increases, and decreasing if its value falls as x increases; this is checked using the sign of the first derivative.
points: Find f'(x) for the given function.
If f'(x) > 0 for all x in an interval, f is strictly increasing there.
If f'(x) < 0 for all x in an interval, f is strictly decreasing there.
Find critical points by solving f'(x) = 0.
Use these points to divide the number line into intervals and test the sign of f'(x) in each.
State the increasing and decreasing intervals clearly as the final answer.
formula: f increasing if f'(x) > 0; f decreasing if f'(x) < 0

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Find f prime x"] --> B["Solve f prime x = 0"]
  B --> C["Mark critical points on number line"]
  C --> D["Test sign of f prime in each interval"]
  D --> E["Write increasing / decreasing intervals"]

example: f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 3. f'(x) = 2x - 4 = 0 at x = 2. For x < 2, f'(x) < 0 so f decreases; for x > 2, f'(x) > 0 so f increases.
tip: Always show the sign chart (number line with + and - marked) as it is directly awarded marks in board papers.

def: A function has a maximum at a point if its value there is greater than nearby values, and a minimum if it is smaller; these are found using the first and second derivative tests.
points: Find f'(x) and solve f'(x) = 0 to get critical (stationary) points.
Find f''(x) at each critical point.
If f''(x) < 0, the point is a point of maximum (maximum value = f(x) there).
If f''(x) > 0, the point is a point of minimum (minimum value = f(x) there).
If f''(x) = 0, the second derivative test fails; use the first derivative sign change instead.
For word problems, also check endpoints if the domain is restricted (closed interval).
formula: f'(x) = 0 gives critical points; f''(x) < 0 means maximum, f''(x) > 0 means minimum

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Find f prime x = 0"] --> B["Get critical points"]
  B --> C["Find f double prime x"]
  C --> D{"Sign of f double prime"}
  D -->|Negative| E["Maximum point"]
  D -->|Positive| F["Minimum point"]

example: f(x) = x^3 - 3x. f'(x) = 3x^2 - 3 = 0 gives x = 1, -1. f''(x) = 6x. At x = 1, f'' = 6 > 0, minimum value f(1) = -2. At x = -1, f'' = -6 < 0, maximum value f(-1) = 2.
tip: State clearly whether it is a maximum or minimum point AND give the maximum/minimum value — both are separately awarded marks.

def: Differentials use dy = f'(x) dx to estimate a small change in a function's value without recalculating it fully.
points: Let y = f(x). Small change in x is denoted dx (or delta x), small change in y is dy.
Formula: dy = f'(x) dx, found using the derivative at the known point.
Approximate new value: f(x + dx) ≈ f(x) + dy.
Choose x as a nearby value where f(x) and f'(x) are easy to compute.
This method avoids direct calculation of roots, powers, etc. for values close to a known point.
Smaller dx gives a more accurate approximation.
formula: dy = f'(x) dx     f(x + dx) ≈ f(x) + f'(x) dx

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Choose known x and f x"] --> B["Find f prime x"]
  B --> C["Compute dy = f prime x times dx"]
  C --> D["f x+dx is approx f x + dy"]

example: Find approximate value of sqrt(26). Take x = 25, f(x) = sqrt(x), f'(x) = 1/(2 sqrt(x)). dx = 1. dy = 1/(2x5) x 1 = 0.1. sqrt(26) ≈ 5 + 0.1 = 5.1.
tip: Pick the nearest perfect square or simple value for x so f(x) and f'(x) are easy — this is key to solving fast.

def: The second derivative test uses the sign of f''(x) at a critical point to decide whether that point gives a maximum, a minimum, or is inconclusive.
points: First find critical points by solving f'(x) = 0.
Compute f''(x) and evaluate it at each critical point.
f''(x) < 0 at that point means the curve is concave down there, so it is a local maximum.
f''(x) > 0 at that point means the curve is concave up there, so it is a local minimum.
f''(x) = 0 means the test fails; need another method (like first derivative sign change) to decide.
This test is faster than checking signs on both sides, when f'' is easy to compute.
formula: If f'(x0) = 0: f''(x0) < 0 gives maximum; f''(x0) > 0 gives minimum

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Solve f prime x = 0 for x0"] --> B["Find f double prime x"]
  B --> C["Evaluate f double prime at x0"]
  C --> D{"Sign at x0"}
  D -->|Negative| E["Local maximum"]
  D -->|Positive| F["Local minimum"]

example: f(x) = -x^2 + 4x. f'(x) = -2x + 4 = 0 gives x = 2. f''(x) = -2, which is negative, so x = 2 is a maximum point with f(2) = 4.
tip: Always compute f''(x) as a formula first, then substitute the critical point value — this reduces calculation errors.
